# The Long Way Home

There is a particular hour — I have caught it in four cities and two decades — when the streets belong to no one and the mind, unmoored from purpose, begins to speak. I found it again last Tuesday, though I hadn't planned to. I had left the house to mail a letter, and then, letter posted, I simply kept going. Past the bakery with its yeasty exhale, past the park where the sprinklers stitched silver thread through dark grass, down a street I had never taken because it went the wrong way. I walked for an hour with nowhere to be, and by the time I turned toward home I had solved nothing, decided nothing, and felt entirely remade.

We have a rich vocabulary for movement with a destination: commute, errand, trek, pilgrimage, expedition. We have almost no good words for movement without one. *Stroll* is too dainty, *wander* too aimless, *flânerie* too French, too nineteenth-century, too much about being seen. What I mean is simpler and older: walking as a way of thinking — or rather, as a way of letting thought happen. The long way home. The wrong turn taken on purpose. The lap around the block that exists only because the block is there.

The Greeks understood this well enough to build a school around it. The Peripatetics, Aristotle's followers, took their name from the covered walkways of the Lyceum, where philosophy was conducted on the move. To philosophize was, quite literally, to walk. Aristotle seems to have believed — and a long line of thinkers after him agreed — that the mind works differently when the legs are working too. There is something about the rhythm of it, the mild and repetitive exertion, that loosens whatever is knotted in us. Sitting at a desk, I can worry a problem like a dog with a bone, chewing the same surface over and over. Walking, the problem comes apart on its own, the way a clenched fist opens when the body finally trusts it is safe.

Thoreau knew this. His essay "Walking" is four parts manifesto and one part weather report, but the conviction underneath is simple: that walking is not exercise, not transportation, but a *vocation*, a sacred sauntering, as he put it, borrowing from a fake etymology he fully endorsed — *sans terre*, without land, without a fixed abode, holy vagrancy. Four hours a day, he said, minimum, and preferably toward the west, toward the coming night, into the wilder edges of the town. He would have despised our step counters, our ten thousand virtuous laps around the same reservoir, our walks that exist to be logged, compared, and atoned for. A walk that is counted is a walk that has already been spent.

Wordsworth walked so much that his neighbors spoke of him as a feature of the landscape, a movable landmark. He composed on his feet. The lines arrived with the mileage, and it is not a metaphor to say that the poems *are* the walks — their long sentences unspooling at the pace of a body moving through Lake District weather, pausing at gates, turning to look back at what it has just passed. You can read "Tintern Abbey" on a treadmill if you like, but you will not hear it. The poem breathes the way a walker breathes, in long even measures, with the occasional catch.

I think about this whenever I see people walking with their chins dipped toward a phone, thumbing the world smaller. I am not interested in scolding them. The phone is a miracle, and I use mine more than I admit. But there is a particular flattening that happens to a walk when it is interrupted every twenty seconds — a flattening of time itself. The walk becomes a series of instants, each one severed from the last, and the landscape outside shrinks to a scenery track playing underneath something more important. What walking offers, when it is allowed to, is the opposite of this: continuity. One thing after another after another, without a highlight reel, without a summary, without a notification that anything important has occurred. The important thing is that nothing important occurs. That is the whole trick.

Because the mind, it turns out, is not a machine for focusing. It is a machine for *roaming*, and it does its best work at the edge of attention — that half-attentive state where you are watching the light on the wet asphalt and also, somewhere underneath, reorganizing your entire understanding of a friendship. Psychologists call it the default mode network, that constellation of brain regions that lights up when we are not concentrating on a task, and one of its specialties is what they call autobiographical planning: the slow, sideways work of making sense of our own lives. This is the network that activates when we walk without a destination. It is, in the most literal neurological sense, the network of getting slightly lost. Every purposeless walk is a session of unpaid, unstructured therapy conducted by a therapist who is also the pavement.

I learned to love the long way home in a city that did not reward it. I was living then in a place built entirely around arrival — wide arterial roads, strip malls receding into the heat haze, sidewalks that appeared and vanished like an afterthought. Walking anywhere was an act of mild deviance. People in cars looked at me the way one looks at a person talking to himself. But that is exactly why I remember those walks with such tenderness. Deprived of the usual justifications — a shop to reach, a friend to meet, a scenic vista to consume — the walking had to justify itself, and it did, again and again, in the currency of small discoveries. A driveway shaded by a jacaranda that had no business growing there. A fence with a hand-painted sign that said DON'T EVEN THINK ABOUT IT in three languages. The particular sound a sprinkler makes at six in the evening in a dry place, which is the sound of a small固执 belief in lawns.

Getting lost, I came to understand, is a skill, and like most skills it has been quietly engineered out of modern life. We are navigated now, constantly, patiently, by a calm voice that has never once been wrong in the way that matters. The voice does not take the long way. The voice does not say, *I wonder what's down that street.* The voice has no interiority, no curiosity, no memory of the time you took this road with someone you no longer speak to. It delivers you to the destination with the efficiency of a fax machine, and you arrive, and you cannot for the life of you remember the journey, because the journey was never allowed to become one.

Compare this to the old way, the way my mother navigated, which was to drive generally in the direction of the place and then ask. Asking was not a failure of navigation; it *was* navigation, a social act, a small theater of directions performed with strangers. Turn where the old gas station used to be. Follow the road past the church and then it's the third left, no wait, maybe the fourth. You arrived not because a system had optimized your route but because a series of small human encounters had, in the aggregate, delivered you. You arrived with stories. You arrived late. You arrived carrying the names of streets you would never need again but would always remember — Oxtongue Lake Road, the Anything Street, the one with the mailbox shaped like a bass.

Night walking is its own discipline, and I recommend it without reservation, with the usual caveats about knowing your city. The night rearranges the familiar. Streets you have walked a hundred times in daylight become provisional, slightly fictional, as if the city were a stage set and you had wandered backstage. Sounds travel differently — a conversation two blocks away arrives intact, unexplained, a fragment of someone else's life deposited at your feet. And the mind, sensing the strangeness, drops its daytime agenda. The worries that seem so structurally important at noon — the email, the dental appointment, the slow catastrophe of the century — lose their chairs and stand awkwardly in the empty street, and then, unnoticed, sit down on the curb and grow quiet.

I have a friend who cannot walk without a podcast, and I love this friend, and I also think something is being missed. Not the content — the content is fine, the content is excellent, some of the best thinking being done today is being done into microphones. What is missed is the *gap*, the open channel, the period at the end of every sentence where something of one's own might surface. We have become a civilization that cannot tolerate the gap. Every elevator, every queue, every red light is an emergency of fill-in. And the walk — the true walk, the one that goes nowhere in particular — is the last widely available gap, the last publicly owned silence. It is being colonized, of course, like all public property. But it holds out. It holds out in the spaces between the earbuds, in the people who still look up.

There is a physics to a good walk that I have tried, without success, to write down. It involves a certain ratio of effort to ease. Too little effort and the mind stays domestic, keeps circling the house, checking the rooms. Too much and the body becomes the whole story — the burning calves, the lungs, the hill that goes on making its single argument. The right effort is the one that occupies the body just enough to set the mind free, the way a mother's heartbeat occupies a held infant. Flat ground is underrated for this reason. Hills get the glory, the views, the accomplishment. But the flat mile is where thought actually happens, the steady green-mile rhythm, the world arriving at the same rate it is being left behind.

I think of a walk I took years ago, in a coastal town in the off-season, when I was in the middle of a period of my life that I would have described then as stalled and now describe, with the benefit of having lived through what came after, as simply *between*. I walked out along the harbor in the early evening. The boats were stacked and shrink-wrapped for the winter, white and ghostly, a fleet in permanent storage. A dog was running figure eights in an empty lot, completely unused, for no one, out of the pure surplus of being a dog. I walked to the end of the pier and stood there while the light went from pewter to ash, and I thought, with no originality whatsoever, *I don't know what I'm doing with my life.* And then I turned around and walked back, and somewhere in the middle of the walk back — I cannot say where, some midpoint between the stacked boats and the lit window of the fish and chips place — the thought changed key. It was the same thought, but it had become a fact rather than an indictment. I don't know what I'm doing with my life. Well. Nobody walking this pier knows what they're doing with their life. The dog certainly doesn't. The winterized boats don't. The light going out over the water doesn't. It was the most comforting thing anyone has ever said to me, and no one said it. The pavement said it. The mile said it.

This is what the long way home is for. Not for solving, not for optimizing, not for the step count, not even for the views. It is for the slow transmutation of private worry into shared fact — the discovery, made over and over because we keep forgetting it, that we are one body among bodies, one walker among walkers, and that the world at three miles an hour is still the world, still sufficient, still lit at the corners. The speed we have gained has not made the world more sufficient. It has made it more skippable, and a skipped world cannot comfort anyone.

So I am writing a small defense of the unmapped mile, the errand extended past its natural end, the street taken because the light was falling on it in a certain way. saunter, Thoreau said, and meant it as a form of prayer. I would settle for something more modest: a form of attention. The letter was mailed. I was late getting back. Nothing was resolved. The night came on, and the sprinklers ran, and somewhere in the middle of it I remembered a thing I had been trying to remember for weeks, which is that I like being alive, and that this liking has almost nothing to do with arriving anywhere, and everything to do with the going — foot after foot after foot, the long way, the unhurried way, the way that is the point.
